cim: Agentic Artificial Intelligence Framework Accelerates Conceptualisation of Health Economic Decision Models
cim_eredeti: Agentic Artificial Intelligence Framework Accelerates Conceptualisation of Health Economic Decision Models
szoveg_eredeti:
Agentic Artificial Intelligence Framework Accelerates Conceptualisation of Health Economic Decision Models

Health economic models serve as foundational analytical tools for evaluating the comparative cost-effectiveness of novel healthcare interventions, providing structured quantitative evidence that directly informs public health policies, national reimbursement decisions, and global market access for medical devices and pharmaceuticals. Developing these models requires synthesizing multidimensional clinical trial data, complex epidemiological registries, disease progression trajectories, and therapy sequencing conventions through rigorous multidisciplinary collaboration involving clinicians, biostatisticians, and specialized health economists. The initial stage of conceptualisation, which establishes the overarching structural architecture and defining clinical assumptions of a decision problem, remains one of the most resource-intensive bottlenecks within health economics and outcomes research. In response to rising pathway complexity across modern clinical practice, researchers have evaluated the feasibility of automating and refining health economic model conceptualisation through an agentic generative artificial intelligence architecture that combines graph-based retrieval-augmented generation, chain-of-thought prompt engineering, and human expert validation across two contrasting clinical case studies.

The traditional human-led conceptualisation process begins with systematic disease characterisation, in which analysts formalize the analytical scope by establishing core Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome parameters alongside explicit institutional perspectives. Health economists subsequently decompose complex decision problems into distinct segments covering disease pathways, discrete health states, and resource utilization categories before iteratively analyzing each component to define baseline assumptions, structural uncertainties, and data requirements. Once these individual components are established, modelers synthesize the pieces into an integrated framework, ensuring that transition rules and comparative clinical assumptions remain methodologically aligned with established health technology assessment standards. However, because this manual progression is exceptionally labour-intensive and can take up to three months of continuous technical work, critical steps are occasionally expedited or restricted, leaving foundational model designs vulnerable to oversimplification or structural gaps that fail to capture real-world treatment realities.

To overcome these systemic bottlenecks, investigators engineered a multi-layered hybrid intelligence architecture grounded in human-in-the-loop methodology, operating on the principle that autonomous algorithmic reasoning must be continuously steered and validated by domain experts. The conceptual framework selected a human-in-the-loop configuration over an alternative artificial-intelligence-in-the-loop arrangement, recognizing that while the latter restricts machine involvement to narrow operational subtasks like automated data extraction or routine mathematical calculations, the former positions artificial intelligence as an active exploratory partner capable of proposing novel state transitions, simulating competing clinical pathways, and flagging internal structural contradictions. Independent human modelers possessing five to twelve years of professional conceptualisation experience provided iterative oversight, verifying that all interim proposals remained clinically justifiable and compatible with health technology assessment principles while allowing the autonomous agent to lead reasoning tasks.

At the reasoning core of the experimental framework, the team utilized OpenAI GPT-5.2 within an external Python programming environment, while noting that the underlying analytical sequence remains model-agnostic and transferable to comparable large language models. The architecture implemented chain-of-thought prompting compounded with self-consistency to mitigate the inherent stochastic instability of open-ended language model generations. Because health economic conceptualisation lacks a single absolute ground truth, self-consistency served as an empirical proxy for structural robustness by issuing identical prompts across five independent parallel reasoning trajectories. Each run generated a distinct step-by-step chain of thought, after which an external language model judge, powered by GPT-5.1, applied a majority-voting consensus protocol to extract the most recurrent health states, directional transitions, and overarching structural configurations across the five sampled iterations, thereby neutralizing idiosyncratic reasoning errors.

Because foundational language models are constrained by general pre-training corpora that lack niche health economic methodologies and granular clinical parameters, the framework incorporated an external retrieval-augmented generation database to infuse domain-specific guidelines into the reasoning loop. Rather than utilizing standard vector retrieval, which treats ingested passages as isolated document fragments, the investigators deployed Microsoft GraphRAG to organize domain knowledge into an interconnected topological network of conceptual nodes and relational edges. This relational graph mapped intricate dependencies between disease progression stages, therapeutic interventions, health utilities, and healthcare cost variables, closely mirroring structured human conceptual memory. Constructed from regional clinical guidelines, health technology assessment frameworks from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence and Canada’s Drug Agency, and published clinical trials, the graph was refined using language model entity extraction and approved by human experts before active querying.

The operational orchestration was governed by an agentic execution layer configured to manage multi-step reasoning through an auditable reason-act-observe loop following the ReAct design pattern. Working through an externalized scratchpad maintained within a structured message buffer, the autonomous agent evaluated problem parameters, identified specific evidentiary gaps, and formulated natural-language queries executed as score-based similarity searches against the GraphRAG repository. The buffer recorded every emitted tool call, intermediate retrieved passage, and subsequent reasoning update, compiling a comprehensive, traceable audit trail accessible to human reviewers. At each discrete junction, the language model determined whether accumulated evidence was sufficient to finalize structural recommendations or whether further retrieval was necessary, cycling iteratively between internal deliberation, contextual evidence retrieval, and logical reassessment before delivering its structured conceptual output.

To evaluate adaptability across sharply contrasting evidence landscapes, the investigators conducted two proof-of-concept case studies that reflected opposing extremes of healthcare information availability. The first case study targeted advanced hormone receptor-positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative breast cancer, representing a data-rich oncology indication with abundant clinical literature, established treatment paradigms, and mature published health economic evaluations. The model utilized published data from the phase three MONALEESA-3 clinical trial assessing ribociclib plus fulvestrant against standard care in post-menopausal women. To prevent data contamination and ensure authentic exploratory problem-solving, researchers explicitly withheld all existing health economic models and health technology assessment submissions from the GraphRAG corpus, restricting retrieval access entirely to clinical trial reports and authoritative institutional appraisal guidelines.
